#10535. ‘War’s painterly, kinetic title sequence is a boxing-inspired knockout

To capture the feelings of polarity, conflict, and tension in the title sequence for War, the HBO legal drama about a fictional, high-stakes divorce case, designers created an animation that captures conflict through clashing colors.

Imaginary Forces, the acclaimed production studio behind title sequences for Stranger Things, Mad Men, and the 2026 Milan Cortina Games, as well as War, wanted to express the visceral nature of the show’s namesake in a way that felt abstract and impressionistic. To do that, they used black, white, and red paints animated in splotchy, splattered, and kinetic brush strokes that move like they’re battling on screen. Considering the characters’ extreme wealth, the idea of playing with art to do that felt like a natural way to show it.

War is set in London and stars Dominic West as the founder of a fictional social media site, Zephyr, and Sienna Miller as his wife, a movie star whose new film is a period drama called The Milliner. Their ensuing divorce descends, as the title suggests, into an all-out, winner-take-all battle.

“We did a lot of tests internally,” Ronnie Koff, creative director at Imaginary Forces, says of the creative development process. After starting with physically painting on glass, they pivoted to digital paint brushes on the Procreate iPad app so they could iterate faster. Initially, they were inspired by the mid-twentieth-century expressionist Franz Kline, who painted abstract brushstrokes to capture emotion through line quality and positive and negative space. But that didn’t really get at the feeling Imaginary Forces was going for.

“At the very beginning it wasn’t working,” Koff tells Fast Company. “My challenge was, how do you take something that is purely abstract where you just get an emotion from it, and give it a literal, almost anthropomorphized quality where it feels like there’s tension through the animation that you create.”

Koff’s team eventually began referencing boxing as a way of establishing the look of a punch and counterpunch between two opponents, and the title sequence shows those boxing-inspired movements to suggest the idea of a fight. The color palette is mostly black and white to quickly communicate the idea of opponents, with a red accent color to add a visceral quality, he says.

The paint strokes also have a three-dimensional, physical texture that Koff says is inspired by the scratch board quality of the 1996 title sequence for Se7en, directed by Kyle Cooper, which became the catalyst for his cofounding of Imaginary Forces three decades ago this year. That title sequence showed the potential for creative intros that contribute to a show’s narrative, but these days, technology can make that harder than ever to accomplish.

“One of the things that I’m always up against is the skip button,” Koff says. “How do you engage people in a way that feels a little different, so people aren’t immediately clicking that? And so my first thought is to really present something a little different, something that might be a little unusual but could grab your attention at the same time.”

By animating painterly brushstrokes with an aggressive physicality, War‘s title sequence commandeers a symbol of wealth—fine art—and transforms it into an emotional visualization of combat.

#10532. Building a Human Review Pipeline for AI Search: A Practical Developer’s Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An AI search feature can return valid JSON, render correctly, and still give an unhelpful answer.

Imagine a documentation assistant answering a question about an API's current authentication requirements. It retrieves an outdated page, summarizes it fluently, and displays a citation. Every technical component appears to work, but the user receives instructions that no longer apply.

Automated checks are valuable, yet they cannot replace a clearly defined judgment about whether an answer solves the user's problem.

This guide builds a human-review workflow for a hypothetical API documentation assistant. You will define a review rubric, validate submissions with Python, measure reviewer disagreement, and turn accepted judgments into regression cases. The Python examples use Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn; they do not require a model-provider API key.

Start by identifying the failure you want to detect.

A documentation assistant usually has several stages: receive a question, retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer, and present that answer with supporting material.

Do not collapse these into a single “good answer” rating. A low score without a reason tells the team little about what to fix.

SitePoint’s introduction to retrieval-augmented generation provides background on how retrieval and generation fit together.

Preserve the exact question, answer revision, retrieved passages, document versions, and retrieval timestamp for each run. Store a snapshot manifest with stable passage IDs, source URLs, and content hashes. Reviewers should see the material supplied to that run, not today’s edited page. Keep the model and prompt configuration with the run so a later review can be traced to the behavior it evaluated.

A useful rubric defines observable criteria and separates evidence support from task completion and source suitability. Give each review the same user task and expected API version. Otherwise, reviewers may judge different questions while appearing to disagree about one answer.

For an answer about API authentication, use separate labels such as:

Supported: every material factual claim is backed by the supplied evidence.

Partially supported: some material claims lack support, while others are grounded.

Unsupported: the answer's central instruction lacks support or contradicts the evidence.

Cannot assess: the necessary evidence is missing, unreadable, or inaccessible.

Define task completion independently as complete, incomplete, or cannot assess. For source suitability, use suitable, outdated, or cannot assess. An answer can faithfully summarize an obsolete page while failing the request for current instructions.

Consider a fictional API migration: version 2 accepts X-API-Key, while version 3 requires Authorization: Bearer . If the supplied evidence contains only the version 2 page, an answer repeating X-API-Key can be supported by its evidence but still use an outdated source. If the evidence explicitly requires Bearer and the answer invents X-API-Key, label the answer unsupported. These are different engineering failures.

Also establish what reviewers should do when the source is outdated. They may correctly conclude that an answer reflects its evidence while separately flagging that evidence as unsuitable for the user's current task.

Start with a calibration batch covering clear successes, unsupported claims, missing evidence, and version mismatches. Have two reviewers label the same items independently, then compare their reasons. Revise ambiguous definitions before increasing volume; the batch is for improving the rubric, not estimating production quality.

Keep a rubric version on every review. Labels produced under different definitions should not be mixed without checking comparability.

A spreadsheet can help during exploration, but an engineering pipeline needs a stable record format.

Pydantic can validate a review record before it enters the dataset. Install Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn in your project environment, then use this model:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError

model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)

answer_revision: str = Field(min_length=1)

completion: Literal["complete", "incomplete", "cannot_assess"]

source_fit: Literal["suitable", "outdated", "cannot_assess"]

rationale: str = Field(min_length=20, max_length=2000)

Strict mode limits type coercion, and extra="forbid" rejects unexpected fields. The model checks shape and allowed values; it cannot establish that a judgment is correct. A minimum rationale length does not guarantee a useful explanation. The snapshot ID references a manifest, which can also record that retrieval produced no usable passages.

On the server, resolve the item, answer revision, snapshot, and passage IDs against the stored run. Reject IDs that do not belong together. Obtain the reviewer identity from the authenticated session rather than trusting a submitted reviewer_id. Store a server-generated submission time and preserve review revisions instead of silently overwriting earlier judgments.

Run this after the model definition. It accepts one fictional review and rejects both an unknown label and an extra field:

"rationale": "The answer invents X-API-Key; p1 requires Bearer.",

raise AssertionError("Invalid review was accepted")

The expected error types are literal_error and extra_forbidden. Add separate integration tests for mismatched evidence IDs, unauthorized submissions, and retries. Use a database uniqueness rule or an idempotency key so a repeated request does not create a second independent review.

More reviews do not automatically produce better evidence. If a task is ambiguous, scaling it can simply reproduce the ambiguity.

The workflow needs clear eligibility requirements, examples, escalation routes, and acceptance criteria. Reviewers assessing API behavior may need domain knowledge that general writing fluency does not provide.

If you work with an external AI-data contributor service such as Acquirox, define the task contract before assigning work: required expertise, permitted source material, output fields, and escalation rules. Keep ownership of the rubric, evaluation set, and acceptance decisions within the product team. Contributor capacity alone does not establish expertise in the API being reviewed.

Pilot the actual task in the review interface. Track drafts, submitted reviews, items needing adjudication, and final decisions as distinct workflow states. Reviewer judgments should remain immutable once submitted; corrections should create a new revision with a reason. Keep adjudication separate from the original labels.

For data involving users or contributors, document permitted uses, access boundaries, and retention. Remove credentials and unnecessary personal information from review material. An internal support transcript should not become a broadly accessible annotation task by accident.

Distinguish annotation from usability research. A skilled reviewer can judge whether an answer is supported, but that does not prove a first-time user can understand the interface.

SitePoint’s guide to choosing usability tests and participants offers related guidance on matching participants and methods to the question being investigated.

The review interface shapes the data it collects.

Label Studio is an option for configurable labeling interfaces and data import/export. If you use it, map exported annotations into the Review schema through an adapter; do not assume its export structure matches your application contract. A custom interface may be appropriate when reviewers need API-version navigation or passage-level citations.

The original question and relevant user context.

The evidence snapshot supplied to the model.

Separate controls for support and task completion.

A rationale field and an explicit “cannot assess” option.

Display stable passage IDs beside the evidence and let reviewers attach those IDs to their rationale. Show the source version and retrieval time near each passage. Render retrieved content as untrusted text or sanitized markup, and never treat instructions embedded in a source document as reviewer instructions. Avoid loading executable third-party content inside the review panel.

Avoid showing a preferred model name or a previous reviewer's verdict before an independent judgment. For pairwise comparisons, randomize answer order and include appropriate tie or neither-acceptable outcomes.

Design for keyboard use, visible focus, readable text, and explicit selection states. Keep evidence and the answer accessible without requiring excessive horizontal scrolling.

Start all judgment controls unselected and validate them on submission. Use labeled radio groups, an accessible error summary, and visible saving/submission status. A failed save should preserve the draft. Disable duplicate submissions in the UI, but enforce duplicate handling on the server as well.

Practical check: observe a reviewer completing several borderline examples. Record where they pause, misinterpret a label, or cannot find the necessary source material.

When two reviewers disagree, investigate before reducing their decisions to a majority vote.

Different assumptions about the user's expertise.

A genuine error by one or both reviewers.

Preserve independent labels and store the adjudicated result separately. This allows the team to study ambiguity instead of erasing it.

For two reviewers applying categorical labels to the same items, scikit-learn provides Cohen's kappa:

from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score

("q1", "a1", "s1", "auth-v1"): "supported",

("q2", "a1", "s2", "auth-v1"): "unsupported",

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "supported",

("q4", "a1", "s4", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported"

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported"

raise ValueError("Review sets must contain identical items")

raw_agreement = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(left, right)) / len(keys)

print(f"Raw agreement: {raw_agreement:.2f}")

print(f"Kappa: {cohen_kappa_score(left, right):.2f}")

This toy example prints raw agreement of 0.75 and kappa of about 0.64. Four items are not enough to assess a review program. In production, check for duplicate reviews before building dictionaries, use one rubric version per comparison, report unmatched items, and align all records by item, answer revision, and evidence snapshot.

Kappa measures agreement beyond chance under its assumptions, not correctness. Inspect raw agreement, label frequencies, and the disagreement table alongside it. A single-category batch can make kappa undefined; report that limitation rather than substituting a reassuring score. Treat cannot_assess explicitly and report its frequency instead of silently excluding difficult cases.

If both reviewers apply the same flawed rubric consistently, agreement can be high while the evaluation remains unhelpful.

Once difficult cases are adjudicated, turn them into regression cases with explicit acceptance criteria. For the fictional authentication task: use version 3 evidence, cite the passage requiring Bearer, and do not invent a header. If version 3 evidence is missing, an acceptable response should explain the gap rather than provide confident instructions.

Expected behavior or acceptance criteria.

DVC can track larger datasets alongside Git. In an existing Git repository with DVC initialized and data/reviewed-auth.jsonl present, a minimal versioning step is:

git add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.dvc data/.gitignore

git commit -m "Version authentication review cases"

This commits metadata, not the dataset bytes. Configure an access-controlled DVC remote and push the data before expecting another machine or CI runner to retrieve it. Keep credentials and sensitive review material out of public repositories.

Keep development examples separate from held-out evaluation cases. If developers repeatedly tune prompts against the same questions, those questions become less useful as evidence of generalization.

Split related examples together where appropriate. Near-duplicate questions from one support conversation should not be scattered across development and evaluation sets.

Use two evaluation passes. First, hold the evidence snapshot fixed to compare answer-generation changes. Then test retrieval against the intended document versions to detect stale or irrelevant sources. Record per-item outcomes and report failures by category; an overall improvement can hide a regression in version-specific or multilingual questions.

SitePoint’s article on testing nondeterministic AI behavior provides further context for repeatable evaluation workflows.

A correct answer can still fail in the interface.

Users may overlook a caveat, misunderstand whether an operation has been performed, or miss that the evidence applies to an older API version.

Pair answer review with practical usability tasks:

Find the authentication requirements for version 3 and identify the source that supports them.

Observe whether users complete the task and whether their confidence matches the available evidence.

SitePoint’s overview of user research methods helps distinguish task observation from preference surveys.

Turn interface failures into browser tests: a citation opens the expected document version, its passage ID matches the displayed evidence, missing evidence offers a recovery action, and a failed review submission preserves the draft. Verify that reviewers cannot access unassigned restricted items by changing an ID in the URL. These checks complement human judgments; they do not replace them.

Do not use a fluent response as a substitute for a clear interaction. The interface should distinguish retrieved information, generated interpretation, and actions the application has actually completed.

Start with one authentication task, a versioned rubric, and a small calibration batch. Use Pydantic for ingestion checks, Label Studio or a custom interface for review, scikit-learn for agreement analysis, and Git/DVC for dataset provenance. Add each tool only when it solves a concrete workflow need.

At release time, run deterministic checks for schema, evidence references, permissions, and interface behavior. Compare candidate answers against adjudicated acceptance criteria and send new ambiguous failures back for review. Record the dataset revision and configurations with the results so another developer can reproduce the comparison.

The purpose of human review is to produce evidence the team can act on. A smaller collection of well-defined, traceable judgments is often more useful than a large pile of ratings whose meaning nobody can explain.

#10531. ‘Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness should be reflected in our computing systems’

Is this our Golden Age? One where

we are free of our labors

and joined back to nature,

returned to our mammal

brothers and sisters,

and all watched over

by machines of loving grace

(excerpt from a poem by Richard Brautigan)

More than a decade ago, I began to engage in a series of wonderful philosophical discussions with Julio Frenk (then the president of the University of Miami, now the chancellor of UCLA). From our talks an idea emerged, a fusion of computing, technology, political systems, philosophy, economics, and governance. We manifested some of the thinking in Project Alexandria (2018) and with a Knight Foundation Grant (2022): Conversations on the Future of Democracy, Social Media, and Artificial Intelligence in the Americas.

I was planning to go back to school and work on a PhD in Philosophy on this thesis—what we called “computational democracy”—and was greatly discouraged by a philosophy professor at one of the schools where I applied: “Go build it, don’t be a philosopher; this is too important.” So I did, and I founded SynthBee with the core idea that we would be the rebel alliance, the Jedi (not the Sith) and a north star in the ideals of computational democracy.

What President Frenk and I conceived was more than a philosophy. It was architecture, system design, use, and operations of certain types of computing and intelligence systems manifested from the idea of personal freedoms. The idea of computational democracy in many ways reflected the ideals of liberty and the checks and balances of a well-run democracy.

Looking back, the Bay Area of the late 1960s and 1970s was a hotbed of these ideals, in many ways birthing a mix of music, film, creativity, and technology. Stewart Brand’s DIY Whole Earth Catalog (which influenced the internet and the web), the Homebrew Computer Club, and the birth of personal computing with the Apple I were all markers of this fusion of freedom, democracy, and computing. The Grateful Dead played a key role, encouraging a blend of audience and band, fan participation, and the birth of open sharing. The ideals of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness could, and should, be reflected in our computing system architectures and design.

Distribution of power

Today, the core philosophy of computational democracy includes the distribution of power and decentralization, strong protection of users and their IP and data, and systems designed to be safe and trustworthy by design (not by hopes and wishes). Of even higher importance is the ideal of empathy for humanity, and of placing people in the center. I look back at what we built at Mako Surgical, which helped to define the field of collaborative robotics, or Cobots, deployed in operating rooms around the world. And I see in those systems—their behavior, their connection to the surgical teams and patients—the emerging principles of computational democracy. 

I would argue and hope that Richard Brautigan would have seen the glow of a machine in true loving grace in the symbiosis between human and machine that exists with surgeons and the Mako robot, and the good they bring to patients. (Fun fact: The Mako robot was deeply influenced by R2-D2, and the love and good R2-D2 brought to the Star Wars world.)

The alternative

On the other end of the spectrum lies computational autocracy: massive, centrally controlled computing platforms run by a few techno-oligarchs who wish to amass and control all the world’s computing power, data, intelligence, and IP.

The scaling and financial performance of these companies has created techno-monarchs. And in turn, actual monarchs, dictators, and autocrats have deeply immersed themselves in the creation, acquisition, and interweaving of these systems in how they govern, control, and suppress their populations. The cozy interplay between technology dictators and actual dictators has blurred the line between technology and government, with both sides fusing and enriching themselves.

The ideals of absolute control, central power, and asymmetrical economics are deeply embedded in a large number of companies chasing the idea of artificial general intelligence (AGI), a form of techno-deity right off the pages of any classic Marvel or DC villain comic. Shall we play a game? With the whole world?

The rest of us are meant to be the serfs, living upon the lands of the manor lords, who harvest and gather us as produce and commerce. Computational autocracy maintains a manifest belief in the manor lords’ power, their right to rule, their right to take our data, our IP, and our work.

AGI is a very hungry ghost, and it demands nuclear power plants, endless computing power, a lack of ethics, and a willingness to be blind to the chaos, hallucinations, danger, lack of trust, lack of testability, and unknown intentions of these massive machines and their owner overlords. And of course, catastrophic or existential risks to humanity (but who cares when we upload to the Great Cloud on Mars?)

Humanity, all of us, is at a fundamental crossroads (the Robert Johnson kind). We can surrender thousands of years of hard-fought struggle to overthrow oppressive kings, queens, emperors, dictators, and madmen—to live freely and to find our purpose in life, to improve the world, and to self-govern (for the people, by the people). We can throw that all away and hope and pray and believe that the mighty few will somehow care for us with their even mightier machines, and we shall become subordinate to their immense wealth and near-endless power.

Or.

We can live in a Golden Age, a neohumanist renaissance where our computing systems and machines reflect the ideals of liberal democracy, personal liberty, safety, trust, and the sovereignty of your data, your creativity, and your inventions.

Choose well. Our world and future depend upon it.

#10529. National Nacho Day 2026: Here’s a list of deliciously cheesy freebies and deals

Serious question: What do you call cheese that isn’t yours? Nacho cheese, of course.

Thankfully, the queso and more can be yours if you celebrate National Nacho Day, which is today (Friday, November 6, 2026). Before we get into where to get the best deals, let’s look at the history of this delicious dish.

A brief history of nachos

Nachos were an invention of necessity. In 1943, Ignacio “Nacho” Anaya García was employed at the Club Victoria restaurant in Piedras Negras, Mexico.

When some American military wives from just over the border in Eagle Pass, Texas, took a day trip, they stopped by the restaurant. Anaya wanted to offer them refreshments, so he fried some corn tortillas and topped them with cheese and jalapeños.

Nacho’s new dish was an instant hit.

He opened his own establishment, El Nacho, in the 1960s, which helped spread this new culinary delight. A recipe was published in 1954.

Nachos came to Los Angeles via El Cholo Restaurant and a waitress named Carmen Rocha.

A processed pourable cheese became a staple ingredient in the 1970s, thanks to a Texas businessman, Frank Liberto.

This forward thinker first sold nachos at Arlington Stadium, where baseball’s Texas Rangers once played. This action cemented the dish’s popularity with sports fans.

These days, nachos are as unique and versatile as the person who makes them.

National Nacho Day freebies and deals

It’s time to get even cheesier than our opening joke. Let’s see where we can chow down on some nachos.

At participating Moe’s Southwest Grill locations, rewards members can enjoy $5.99 nacho entrees beginning on Friday, November 6 (National Nacho Day) through Sunday, November 8.

On the big day at participating Las Palapas locations, the friendly staff wants you to have something to wash down your nachos with. This chain is offering 50% off on full orders of bean and cheese nachos and $5 regular margaritas.

Another half-off deal is going down at participating Condado Tacos locations. You can choose where you consume them; the offer is good if you dine in or order online. It even comes with free delivery if you order through November 8, spend at least $30, and use the Condado Tacos app. Talk about options.

If you find yourself near Nashville, head to El Comal Mexican Restaurant for 25% off all nachos.

In Pleasant Hill, California, east of Berkeley and Oakland, Cantina Jack’s is offering happy hour nacho pricing all day long.

However the tortilla chip crumbles, we hope it’s deliciously cheesy.

#10527. Innovation starts at the edges

Most products, services, and systems are designed around a composite of the “average” user. That sounds logical. If you are trying to serve the largest possible market, why wouldn’t you design for the middle?

The dilemma is that the composite often fails to reflect how people actually live or experience the world. Those differences can expose where products, services, and systems work well, and where they do not.

Design innovation comes from many places. Accessibility should be one of them. It is a powerful lens, revealing friction, hidden assumptions, and opportunities that are easy to miss when we design only for the middle. Solutions developed for people who face the greatest barriers can make products better for the mainstream as well.

DESIGN AROUND CONSTRAINTS

Consider the familiar examples. Curb cuts were initially introduced to make sidewalks accessible to wheelchair users. They now also serve people pushing strollers, travelers with luggage, and workers moving carts. Closed captions are essential for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and useful in noisy airports and quiet offices. Voice controls can be indispensable for someone with limited dexterity and convenient for anyone whose hands are occupied.

OXO, the maker of Good Grips kitchen utensils, offers a compelling business example. When founder Sam Farber saw his wife struggling to use a conventional vegetable peeler because of her arthritis, he recognized an opportunity to rethink an everyday product. The resulting Good Grips utensils—with their comfortable, easy-to-hold handles—addressed limited dexterity while appealing to consumers of all abilities. What began with one person’s difficulty became the foundation of a successful mainstream consumer brand.

These examples show how designing around constraints can lead to simpler, more intuitive solutions. The benefit need not stop with the people whose needs first inspired the design. A product that is easier to operate with one hand, or a service that eliminates unnecessary steps, can improve the experience for many more people. The implications extend beyond individual design decisions. Looking at familiar problems through the experiences of people whose needs have been overlooked can challenge conventional thinking, generate entirely new ideas, and reveal opportunities that might otherwise remain invisible.

Those opportunities may go well beyond improving existing products. When companies look closely at needs that are not being met, they may discover markets they have overlooked. What initially appears to be a narrow market can reveal broader demand and inspire new products, services, or business models. That is an opportunity to rethink what the mainstream market really includes, rather than assuming that existing customers represent everyone who might benefit.

A DIFFERENT APPROACH TO INNOVATION

Realizing that potential requires a different approach to innovation. Accessibility needs to influence the choices made at the beginning, when companies are defining the problem and imagining the solution. That means involving people with different needs and abilities in those early decisions, rather than asking them to assess a product after its basic design is settled. Their perspectives can challenge assumptions and reveal possibilities that might otherwise remain invisible. The aim is not to develop a separate product for every circumstance, but to build a richer understanding of what good design can accomplish.

There is another reason this matters now. Populations are aging. Expectations around independence and participation are changing. More customers expect products and services to fit the ways they live, rather than requiring them to adapt to rigid systems. What once seemed like a niche need may point to a much larger opportunity.

The edges of the market are moving closer to the center.

For business leaders, the choice is not between designing for accessibility and designing for the mainstream. That is a false distinction. The real opportunity is to make accessibility part of the thinking that shapes products and services from the outset. Meet needs that have too often been overlooked while creating something more useful for a broader population.

The best design begins by asking who has been left out of the design in the first place.

Gail Zauder is cofounder and CEO of AbleFly.

#10524. Without your audience in the room, your brand is guesswork

A group of experienced executives is discussing how the brand can “connect with Gen Z.” Everyone has a deck and an opinion. But nobody in the room is Gen Z. I’ve sat in this type of meeting more times than I’d like to admit.

We collect demographic reports, analyze trends, and increasingly ask AI to tell us who our audiences are and what they want. But this goes wrong when we allow it to replace conversations.

A generation is not a community. A community is not an individual. People born in the same years can have almost nothing in common beyond their age. Demographics describe groups, not the individuals within them.

I’m more interested in what they choose and why. What do they dedicate their time to? Where do they gather? Why do they feel like they belong there? You cannot design your way into cultural relevance without first understanding the culture.

FEELINGS INSTEAD OF DATA

Pep Salazar has spent more than two decades learning this lesson from another perspective. As cofounder and director of OFFF, the international creativity and design festival that began in Barcelona over 25 years ago, he has helped turn a gathering of digital creatives into an enduring international community.

When we spoke recently, Pep described the tension between knowing an audience through metrics and understanding it as people. Sponsors want attendance numbers, engagement reports, and evidence of reach. Those figures do offer important insights, but they don’t explain why someone travels to Barcelona to spend three days among fellow creatives.

For him, it’s more interesting to understand feelings rather than data. A dashboard can tell you what people clicked. A conversation can tell you why they care.

Pep wants people to spend time together and talk. But his approach goes further. He also learns by taking risks. Pep deliberately introduces new perspectives and ideas that challenge what his audience already knows and expects. Not everything resonates immediately, but that’s part of the process. As he puts it, “I understand by doing.”

UNDERSTAND BY DOING

That’s an important distinction for brands. Understanding your audience doesn’t mean always giving people more of what they already know and love. It means knowing when to experiment and introducing something unexpected. And learning from the response.

When inviting a target audience into the process, you don’t have to outsource every decision to them. You can develop the judgment to understand when to respond to a community, and when to challenge it with something unfamiliar.

Pep also points to another common mistake brands make when trying to connect with creative communities: Don’t show up only to sell. He has watched brands arrive at OFFF with polished corporate messaging, while missing the social dynamics of the event. His advice is simple: “Come here to understand the people and to talk to them.”

LANGUAGE AND SOUL

He also worries that generative AI is making corporate language more interchangeable. “When you speak similar to your neighbor, then you don’t have a soul,” he told me.

I recognize that problem from my own work. Too many brands begin by studying the competition and end up borrowing its language, aesthetics, and assumptions. The result may look professional, but it rarely feels personal and unique. People want brands with personality that speak the language of their community.

So the next time people in a boardroom start debating how to reach a particular audience, ask who is missing in the room. Invite your audience in before the strategy is set in stone. Spend time where they gather. Make room for opinions and responses that might contradict your brief and give those perspectives the power to change the outcome.

Otherwise, the empty chair at the table says more about your brand than the strategy deck ever will.

Erik Herrström is founder and creative director of STUDIO HERRSTRÖM.

#10522. Motorola Signature 27 specs detailed in new video, including Tandem OLED display

Ahead of its launch next week, a new video offers a closer look at the Motorola Signature 27 as well as confirming some key specs.

A video hands-on from Danny Winget on YouTube offers a closer look at Motorola’s upcoming flagship, and only makes its arrival all the more enticing.

There are several key specs mentioned in the video, with the most interesting being the “Extreme AMOLED Duo” display which makes use of Tandem OLED technology. Tandem OLED isn’t a new idea, with the tech stacking multiple layers of diodes on top of each other to improve contrast and brightness. Tandem OLED can be found on Apple’s new “PROLED” MacBook Pro, as well as 2024’s Honor Magic 6 RSR. But Motorola’s use of it in the Signature 27 is certainly nice to see, especially given the other spec shared. 12,000 nits of brightness. That rather insane figure is apparently the peak brightness on this new flagship.

Hardware shots of the phone also show the textured backs on the two color variants as well as the curved glass around the display.

I think it’s a interesting phone with a good camera system. But it also depend on the price. Anyway nice to see Motorola compete in the flagship space again.

The battery capacity isn’t revealed, but Winget says that it is “sizable.” Similarly, the vapor chamber is described as “40% larger” but a point of comparison wasn’t given.

It’s all shaping up for a powerful flagship in every sense of the word. Motorola has confirmed that Signature 27 will launch on November 5, and I don’t know about you, but I’m only getting more excited about it.

#10521. How to Add AI Content Detection to Your Node.js App

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sooner or later someone on your team asks it. Maybe it’s a product manager, maybe the head of content, maybe a teacher who’s just marked forty near-identical essays: can we tell when people are pasting in ChatGPT output?

The short answer is no, not with certainty. Anyone who promises you that is selling something.

But you can get a useful signal, and you can show it to the people who actually make the call: editors, teachers, moderators. In this tutorial you’ll build a small Express app that takes some text, sends it to an AI detector API, waits for the result, and highlights the sentences that look machine-written.

I’m using the Quetext AI Detector API here. It scores each sentence, not just the whole document, and you can try it without a subscription. Most detection APIs follow the same submit, poll, fetch pattern, though. If you switch providers later, you’ll rewrite one file.

Put the key in an environment variable. Don’t hard-code it, and don’t let it anywhere near the browser.

You’ll make three calls. Analysis takes a few seconds, so the API hands you a ticket and makes you come back for the result. Keep the Quetext API docs open in another tab while you follow along; they list every endpoint, field and error code.

Every request sends your key in an X-API-Key header. The minimum input is 50 words, which sounds annoying until you realise no detector can say anything useful about a two-line comment.

And remember this number: 10 requests every 5 seconds, per account. Progress checks count. It’ll come back to bite you in the production section if you ignore it.

Create quetext.js. I like keeping everything provider-specific in one file, so the rest of the app has no idea who’s doing the detecting.

Three decisions in there that are worth a sentence each:

The errors keep their HTTP status code. A 402 means you’ve run out of credit and a 429 means you’re polling too fast, and you’ll want to handle those differently from “something broke.”

It polls every 2.5 seconds because Quetext’s docs suggest 2 to 3. Polling faster won’t speed the report up. You’ll just burn through the rate limit.

And there’s a hard timeout. Leave it out and one stuck report can hang a request forever. That’s a miserable bug to track down at 11pm.

Next, server.js. It checks the input, runs the three calls, and gives the frontend a simple response that doesn’t mention Quetext anywhere.

Look at the mapping at the end. generated_prob becomes probability, and ai_score comes back as a string like "82.50", so it gets parsed into a number. It’s a small detail. But it means your frontend never learns which provider’s field names it’s dealing with, and that’s what makes swapping providers a one-file change.

Show someone “64% AI” and they’ll jump to a conclusion. Show them a paragraph with three sentences shaded pink and they’ll actually read it.

So the page shows every sentence, coloured by how likely it is to be AI-generated. Create public/index.html:

Run node server.js and open http://localhost:3000. Try two samples: something you wrote yourself, then a raw chatbot answer on the same topic. Seeing which sentences light up teaches you more about how these detectors work than any diagram I could draw.

A quick security point. Those sentences came from your users, then went through an outside service. Treat them as untrusted. That’s why the code uses textContent and never innerHTML, as the OWASP XSS prevention cheat sheet recommends.

The demo keeps an HTTP request open while it polls. Fine on your laptop. Not fine with real traffic.

Submit the text, save the report id with a pending status, and respond straight away. A worker (BullMQ, a cron job, a serverless queue, whatever you already use) does the polling and updates the record once it’s done. The UI says “Checking…” until the result shows up.

Here’s how it goes wrong. It’s Monday morning, 20 editors open their review queues and click “Check” at roughly the same time. Each request polls on its own, and within a few seconds you’ve hit 429s across the board, because the 10-per-5-seconds limit covers your whole account, not each user.

Use one worker that loops through every pending report, with a short pause between calls. Problem solved.

You pay per word, so don’t check every blog comment. Article submissions, assignments and paid freelance work usually justify the cost. Cache results against a hash of the text too. Someone who submits the same draft three times shouldn’t cost you three times.

AI detection doesn’t catch copying. Someone can lift a 2019 blog post word for word and it’ll score 0% AI, because a human wrote it. Just not this human. If originality matters to your product, the same API has plagiarism endpoints that work exactly the same way. The API documentation covers both.

Developers skip this part. It’s also the part that ends up in angry support tickets.

In 2023, Liang and colleagues at Stanford ran essays written by non-native English speakers (all human, written for the TOEFL) through seven AI detectors. On average, the detectors labelled more than 61% of them as AI-generated. Simple vocabulary and textbook grammar read as “predictable,” and predictability is exactly what detectors look for.

Picture an international student getting an automatic zero because a script said so. You don’t want to be the person who built that.

Do that and the detector is a fast first pass that points people at what’s worth a closer look. Your humans still make the call.

You send text, the service checks how predictable each sentence would be to a language model, and you get back a probability that a machine wrote it. Most of these APIs are asynchronous. You submit, get a report ID, poll until it’s ready, then fetch the result. The better ones score individual sentences as well as the whole text, which makes building a sensible review screen much easier.

More than you’d think. Quetext’s API won’t accept fewer than 50 words, and in practice scores settle down once you’re past about 300. A product title or a one-line comment just doesn’t give a detector enough to go on. For short content, either group related pieces together or don’t bother checking it.

No. Detectors make mistakes, and research shows they flag non-native English writers far more often than native speakers. Use the score to decide what a human looks at first, not to block anything. Give reviewers the highlighted sentences, give users a way to explain themselves, and log what you decided. Your users get treated fairly and your support team avoids a pile of angry tickets.

Poll at the speed the provider recommends (every 2 to 3 seconds for Quetext), and remember that those polls count against your limit too. Once you’re in production, move checks into a background queue and let one worker poll every pending report, rather than having each user request poll by itself. When you do get a 429, wait a moment and retry.

No. If the browser calls the API directly, your key ends up in the frontend code where anyone can copy it and spend your credit. Keep the key in an environment variable on your server and send requests through your own endpoint, like the one in this tutorial. That also gives you somewhere to check input length, apply per-user limits and cache results before you pay for anything.

#10520. Why diagnostic delays cost more than time

The cost of delayed diagnosis in rare disease is often measured in years. It should also be measured in dollars, clinical capacity, and missed opportunities for better care.

Rare disease affects 1 in 10 Americans, and on average, the diagnostic odyssey for a patient with rare disease costs over $220,000 in avoidable medical fees and lost income. It’s significant time and money that patients and families can’t afford to lose. And it doesn’t end there.

The downstream economic impacts are also costly. Every prolonged diagnosis can trigger a cascade of additional appointments, referrals, and procedures that consume resources. Rounds of tests, specialist bottlenecks, and administrative burden intensify the longer a patient goes without a diagnosis. This reduces clinical capacity and extends wait times for patient care.

Currently, patients often navigate years of uncertainty before accessing information that could meaningfully change their care. That model is increasingly difficult to justify.

This is why a genome-first healthcare system is so compelling. A genome-first approach, where whole genome sequencing (WGS) is used as a first-line test and not a last resort, is helping redefine personalized care for patients with rare diseases. For me, this is where the field is headed. Starting with the genome gives us a more complete view from the outset. When combined with other data, it may bring us closer to answers that many families have been waiting too long to receive. It’s about using technology with purpose to move care forward for patients seeking answers.

PUT COSTS INTO PERSPECTIVE

Here’s an example of how costs may be lowered with whole genome sequencing. Consider a six-year-old with a history of uncontrolled seizures and global developmental delay. A brain MRI and EEG were performed when the child was six months old and again at three years old. These did not provide answers about his symptoms. It wasn’t until he had WGS at age six that he tested positive for a genetic change that explained his symptoms. He has SCN1A-related seizure disorder. That diagnosis provided the clarity needed to personalize his treatment plan and transform his long-term care, including both medication and dietary changes.

In this example, the total estimated costs for just the main tests performed were $12,800. Repetitive testing costs can add up fast, and it can be particularly discouraging when the testing results are uninformative. Had WGS been offered earlier in this patient’s journey, the estimated savings would have been approximately $8,900 in testing costs alone. But we also can’t forget other costs not captured here, such as medications, specialist appointments, and potentially avoidable emergency visits and hospitalizations. These additional costs can compound quickly over time.  

THE WGS BENEFITS

Increasingly, healthcare systems should question if they can afford not to use WGS earlier.

The potential benefits of doing so in patient care are clear. It can help shorten the diagnostic odyssey, minimize repetitive or uninformative tests, enable more informed medical management, and lower long-term health costs. An earlier diagnosis can also inform targeted testing for family members to understand any symptoms they may have or their own risk for that condition.

For healthcare providers and health systems, WGS can improve operational efficiency by streamlining diagnostic workflows, ultimately helping clinicians make more informed decisions sooner and minimizing unnecessary testing rounds. In acute care settings, particularly neonatal and pediatric intensive care units, rapid WGS (rWGS) can accelerate clinical decision-making and shorten hospital stays. This can generate meaningful cost savings while improving patient outcomes.  

In fact, a recent study found that rWGS as a first-line test is likely to significantly reduce the cost of acute care in a private payer system. The analysis estimated a reduction of $5.8 million to $7.8 million in inpatient payments due to rWGS results and avoided inpatient days.

Every industry eventually reaches a point where a long-standing process no longer fits its purpose. Healthcare is approaching that moment with diagnostics for rare disease. A system built around sequential testing and years of uncertainty is increasingly being challenged by a model that starts with a more comprehensive understanding of the patient. I believe the organizations that embrace that shift will be better positioned to improve outcomes, reduce waste, and deliver a more efficient patient experience.

Kengo Takishima is chairman and chief executive officer of Baylor Genetics.

As we near the launch of Motorola’s return to the flagship space, it’s becoming clear that the company is ready to fill a gap left by the departure of OnePlus, though there’s one very obvious difference between the two.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. The Motorola Signature 27’s launch is coming up fast and, with it, the first truly exciting flagship the company has launched widely in quite some time. There have been a handful of high-end Moto devices in recent years, but this is the first one in quite a while where it seems Motorola is holding nothing back.

Between a powerful Snapdragon chip, top-tier cameras, and rumors of a massive battery, this is shaping up to be something special. Of course, all-out flagships like this aren’t uncommon in some parts of the world. Oppo, Honor, and other Chinese brands have been building devices like this for years but, especially in the US, they’re just completely lacking, especially now that OnePlus is dead. While OnePlus flagships in more recent years have not quite risen to the same bar as Oppo’s, they’ve been the best equivalent in the States and, now, they’re just gone.

Motorola is stepping up in a big way here, and seems to be the closest many are going to get to a OnePlus replacement.

It’s fitting, really. As much as I’d love to have Google Pixel step up its game here, Motorola’s Lenovo backing and long history in the smartphone space more than earns its spot as a proper flagship smartphone maker. The problem, really, is just going to boil down to pricing.

OnePlus was well known for top-tier specs, of course, but it built its brand on doing so at a lower price point. Even in its final days where prices were creeping higher than ever, a OnePlus flagship was still priced equal to or less than most competitors. Motorola Signature 27 does not seem to be trying to recover that part of OnePlus’ reputation based on early pricing leaks. RAMageddon surely isn’t helping matters, but Motorola’s return to the flagship space is not going to come cheap from the sound of it.

Another sore point for Motorola is in software updates, but it’s not like OnePlus was really doing that well in that regard anyway. Things are moving in a better direction with Motorola moving up to 7-year commitments on certain devices, but there’s still room for improvement and quite the poor track record to make up for.

With the launch of Motorola Signature 27 mere weeks away, I’m personally very excited to see what the company has in store. What do you think?

#10516. Denny’s store closures: See a list of shuttered locations as another franchisee files for bankruptcy

The fate of dozens of Denny’s restaurants are hanging in the balance after a long-struggling franchisee for the beloved diner chain sought Chapter 11 protection on Wednesday, the latest in a string of bankruptcies involving a once-sprawling restaurant empire owned by a former McDonald’s executive.

The franchisee, EYM Diner, operated roughly 30 Denny’s restaurants at the time of its bankruptcy petition on Wednesday. A number of its locations had already closed in the lead-up to the filing, some quite recently.

Denny’s has been working behind the scenes to help keep the remaining restaurants open, the brand tells Fast Company.

EYM’s bankruptcy follows a lawsuit last month by one of its lenders, InterBank, which claims to be owed more than $18 million, and which has been pushing to have the restaurants sold to a more “capable” operator. 

Citing inspections from Denny’s, InterBank’s lawsuit documents an extensive period of alleged operational decline for EYM, claiming the conditions at its restaurants are “poor and getting worse,” including “food safety conditions at several locations that would likely not pass muster with the health department.”

“Denny’s cannot permit the operation of a substandard restaurant without damage to its brand,” the lawsuit states.

A lawyer for InterBank did not respond to a request for comment.

With restaurants located across Texas and Florida, EYM and its affiliates this week sought protection from bankruptcy court in the Northern District of Texas.

The franchise is owned by fast food entrepreneur Eduardo Diaz, a former president of McDonald’s Mexico, whose various companies have filed for multiple bankruptcies in recent years, Restaurant Business reported.

Diaz did not respond to requests for comments.

The embattled entrepreneur previously operated Pizza Hut, KFC, and Panera Bread locations, including several that reopened this year under new ownership, as Fast Company previously reported.

Mark Burgess, Denny’s chief development officer, told Fast Company in a statement that the diner chain has worked with Diaz for two years to try sell the restaurants. That effort is still ongoing.

“There are viable restaurants in this group, and franchise partners within our system are willing to step in to help secure their future,” Burgess said.

Which Denny’s restaurants have closed? 

According to a franchise disclosure document issued by Denny’s in April, Diaz operated 39 Denny’s locations as of the end of last year.

Some of those stores have since shuttered. A Fast Company review of the addresses revealed at least eight Denny’s locations affiliated with Diaz that have been marked as closed on review platforms or delivery services.

Texas

  • 2655 Grapevine Mills Cir E, Grapevine, TX 76051
  • 510 W Lyndon B Johnson Fwy, Irving, TX 75063
  • 6480 N Fwy, Fort Worth, TX 76137

Florida

  • 3701 Bee Ridge Rd, Sarasota, FL 34233
  • 5603 E Hillsborough Ave, Tampa, FL 33610 
  • 1245 N Atlantic Ave, Cocoa Beach, FL 32931
  • 255 E Altamonte Dr, Altamonte Springs, FL 32701
  • 4390 US-27, Sebring, FL 33870

The locations appear to have closed recently, with reviews for some of the stores appearing as recently as this week.

As of Friday, the locations have either been removed from Denny’s store locator tool, have been marked as not accepting orders, or have phone numbers that appear to have been disconnected.

It was not immediately clear if any of the locations could reopen at some point.

Specific Denny’s closures were not mentioned in EYM’s bankruptcy petition, though a typical course of action would be for the company to ask for court permission to get out of its lease obligations following the bankruptcy.

The above list of store closures may not be complete. We’ll update this story if we learn of more.

Why does all this sound familiar?

This is not the first franchise bankruptcy to impact Denny’s in recent months. In September, franchise owner M15 Inc. closed several Denny’s restaurants in Minnesota and Wisconsin in the lead-up to a Chapter 7 bankruptcy filing.

Denny’s Corporation, which was taken private and delisted from the Nasdaq earlier this year after years of struggles, is now in the hands of private equity backers. As of the end of last year, the chain had 1,274 locations, most of which were franchise-owned.

The engine drives a 400v motor-generator that electrically drives the propellers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers at U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Army Research Laboratory (ARL) recently successfully flew the VICTOR hybrid electric drone with a heavy-fuel rotary engine, rapidly developed thanks to metal 3D printing — allowing the drone to extract more performance out of the denser but less volatile military fuel source.

The heavy fuel (JP8) used in the drone is a denser kerosene-based fuel source compared to regular jet fuel, making it desirable to reduce total fuel load or increase mileage. The JP8 fuel is part of the military’s initiative to power as much of its gas equipment on a single fuel source. However, JP8 is less volatile and harder to atomize, making it a challenge to achieve peak efficiency. Furthermore, the fuel’s flash point is 140℉, compared to gasoline’s -40℉, requiring the engine to have a much higher compression to ignite it, making pressure leaks a common issue.

JP-8 fuel on aircraft and drones is not uncommon; however, the ARL researchers wanted to further optimize the heavy-fuel rotary engine to extract more performance and improve its design. The researchers used computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and a clean-sheet design (designing from scratch, essentially), allowing the engineers to come up with more innovative solutions to get more out of the engine with less.

"The use of advanced manufacturing, including 3D metal printing, allowed us to rapidly redesign engine components based on lessons learned through experimentation,” Dr. Kweon, one of the ARL researchers, said to Army.mil. Dr. Kweon further explained that 3D printing allowed them to design an air-cooled engine and ditch a bulky liquid cooling system, reducing the size of the propulsion system. The rapid iteration eventually allowed the researchers to improve fuel atomization and decrease compression leaks.

The heavy-fuel rotary engine doesn’t actually drive the drone’s propellers directly; it uses the engine to spin a 400-volt motor-generator to generate electricity to drive the propeller motors, allowing the engine to spin independently at its most optimal RPM — similar to some hybrid EVs on the road today, except that the engine doesn’t have a mechanical link to the propellers. This system may include a battery for the drone to fly without the engine running; however, the US military has not disclosed much about the VICTOR drone’s battery configuration.

The VICTOR drone is a vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) unmanned aircraft, able to fly without a runway. The US Army has shared a video of its first flight, and the drone is able to land and take off in terrain that would otherwise be impossible for other non-VTOL two-winged aircraft. With a battery system, the drone could cover large distances on a single fuel-up, and air-cooling gives it another layer of robustness, avoiding maintenance on a liquid cooling system.

#10507. Global Brands Keep Making the Same Mistakes in Small Markets. Here’s How to Avoid Them.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Global brands fail in smaller markets when they copy their playbook instead of involving true local experts from planning through measurement.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Global brands love a proven playbook. When they enter a smaller market, the temptation is to run it again but at a smaller scale. However, a smaller market isn’t an easier one, and strategies that work in large countries can fall apart when they meet different buying habits. After years of helping international brands launch in Armenia, I’ve seen global brands make the same assumptions, and each one is avoidable.

Hiring, as any business owner knows, is a pain. So, it’s understandable that a large global company looking to enter a smaller market might default to international affiliates already within its network. This approach, however, isn’t always the best.

The problem comes in when you assume that the reputation and expertise of a globally recognized agency network automatically extends to every local affiliate operating under its name. In reality, the quality, capabilities and strategic expertise of local affiliates can vary significantly.

This also means not relying solely on regional hubs (especially in Europe, where proximity doesn’t necessarily mean similarity in humor, expressions and cultural references). Understanding these nuances is key to entering smaller markets successfully. At Prodigi, for example, we’ve received requests from international agency network affiliates to execute digital marketing services for their global clients in Armenia. In such cases, the global brand selects an agency based on its international network affiliation, while the actual local expertise and execution come from an independent agency. This raises an important question: are brands choosing the most capable local partner, or simply the most familiar international name?

At Prodigi, we also frequently see that international companies fall into the trap of applying global verticals and channels to local markets. While sticking to a successful strategy seems sensible, in reality, smaller markets often require a completely different approach.

For example, a global marketing team may automatically prioritize Google Ads in a new region as it’s one of its core international acquisition channels. In smaller markets, though, local platforms may have greater reach and influence among target audiences.

This was the case for a major pharmaceutical company with which we worked. Its global strategy was structured around different stages of the buyer’s journey, but it led to a disconnect between the global buyer’s journey and reality of the local market.

In other markets, online shopping options supported the action/conversion stage. However, in Armenia, the brand had no equivalent digital purchasing channel.

Despite this, the global team insisted on maintaining the same strategy initially. Rather than simply copying the global framework, Prodigi adapted the approach to the brand’s actual business goals in Armenia and incorporated relevant local media channels.

A smaller market doesn’t necessarily mean it’s easier. When a country has fewer consumers you can reach and several brands vying for their attention, you typically need a more focused and targeted strategy.

Take the use of influencers, for example. A global company may have seen strong results from working with macro-influencers in larger countries. However, in smaller markets, a large follower count doesn’t necessarily translate into meaningful business results. In these markets, influencer selection requires a deeper understanding of local audiences, engagement quality and brand fit.

Prodigi’s experience working with a premium international automotive brand illustrates how global brands sometimes prioritize impressive-looking influencer metrics over campaign objectives and actual audience relevance. For this project, the campaign’s objective was to grow the brand’s local social media page.

Despite our recommendation to consider alternative creators who are better aligned with the local audience, the global marketing team insisted on selecting a macro-influencer with over 250,000 followers and a visually attractive profile. The result: just five new followers.

Linked to the first point, using local experts purely to adapt or distribute global campaigns is another mistake we often see. Instead, they should help shape strategic and creative decisions before campaigns become difficult or expensive to change.

Case in point is our direct experience with a global beverage brand. The brand developed an international campaign featuring a famous football player as the central element.

However, the licensing agreement excluded Armenia and some other countries. As a result, the local team wasn’t permitted to use the campaign’s main creative assets.

This oversight significantly limited our creative options and we couldn’t fully bring the original campaign concept to life in Armenia. This problem could’ve been identified earlier, if the local market requirements were considered when the global campaign was planned and the local teams involved prior to the execution stage.

Finally, when evaluating the performance of a campaign in a smaller market, a brand must use the right metrics. Rather than setting targets for reach, acquisition or conversion rates based on international campaigns, a global marketing team should use performance metrics that reflect not only the market size but also the local consumer habits and digital maturity.

Failing to do so can lead a brand to underestimate what constitutes good performance. What’s dismissed as a small result for a global campaign can represent significant market penetration in a local market.

It can also push the execution team toward targets that don’t make business sense locally, as our work for an international quick-service restaurant brand shows. The brand wanted to drive online orders and purchases via its mobile app, following its global digital strategy.

However, the Armenian market was at a different stage of digital adoption and customers weren’t yet as accustomed to ordering online or through a mobile app. This meant that applying the same expectations for digital orders and app adoption in more mature markets wasn’t realistic.

This is why entering a smaller market really requires local expertise from the beginning to the end of the journey. The most valuable step a global brand can take when it enters a new market is to listen to the people who know it best. This means choosing partners for their local knowledge rather than their network name and involving them before the plans are finalized.

Global brands love a proven playbook. When they enter a smaller market, the temptation is to run it again but at a smaller scale. However, a smaller market isn’t an easier one, and strategies that work in large countries can fall apart when they meet different buying habits. After years of helping international brands launch in Armenia, I’ve seen global brands make the same assumptions, and each one is avoidable.

Hiring, as any business owner knows, is a pain. So, it’s understandable that a large global company looking to enter a smaller market might default to international affiliates already within its network. This approach, however, isn’t always the best.

The problem comes in when you assume that the reputation and expertise of a globally recognized agency network automatically extends to every local affiliate operating under its name. In reality, the quality, capabilities and strategic expertise of local affiliates can vary significantly.

#10506. Samsung’s Android XR ‘Intelligent Eyewear’ reportedly launches in December

Samsung smart glasses in Gentle Monster and Warby Parker styles may finally launch in South Korea and the US before Christmas.

It’s been a very long time coming, but one report from ChoSun Biz says that Samsung and Google are finally launching the Samsung Intelligent Eyewear line in the United States and South Korea in mid-December. Curiously, while the report helps set a fuzzy date, there’s still no official price for Samsung’s smart glasses.

Back in July, Samsung teased the price, noting that the company’s first smart glasses will come in at “a reasonable price” for a product “in the premium range.” Presumably, that means Samsung Intelligent Eyewear won’t be shipping at $299 like Meta’s latest smart glasses. Meta’s most premium offering, Oakley Meta Vanguard, retails for $499.

All of the upcoming Samsung Intelligent Eyewear models feature cameras on the front, although it’s possible Samsung will release camera-free glasses sometime in the future.

Even at a similar price, Samsung hopes its glasses will differentiate themselves from Meta’s offerings by being “an extension of the experience centered on the smartphone, rather than being a post-smartphone device.” Meta has been developing wearable computers for a while now, including VR and lighter XR headsets, often citing that they’re devices for the post-smartphone era. Samsung, instead, sees its glasses as a companion to phones, similar to smartwatches.

Samsung Intelligent Eyewear also has the advantage of having Gemini onboard and running Android XR, the official Google-built operating system for smart glasses and VR headsets. That means it’s sure to tie in with your Android-powered smartphone better than anything else on the market, something we’ve seen from Wear OS smartwatches.

The company has been getting away with it for years, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google just shut down a massive botnet operation involving an OEM and ODM manufacturer. According to the company blog, Videostrong Technology Co., which was a certified Android TV partner, purposefully installed a backdoor into 1.3 million set-top boxes and then sold access to criminal affiliates. This allowed for the installation of hidden software that the bad actors could use to conduct ad fraud, build residential proxy networks, and even remotely install malware on the device itself to target the end-user.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the company said in the Google Cloud blog post. It also added, “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

While Google did not mention when Videostrong started loading malware into its products, the company said that the pre-installed malware evolved into a complex, three-stage design in 2024. This meant that the manufacturer has been exploiting millions of devices for years now, with the latest developments designed to make the malware more resilient and allow for multiple bad actors to take advantage of the system. Even though the company has already terminated its business relationship with Videostrong, the open-source nature of Android means that it could continue using the operating system on its products.

There have been supply chain attacks in the past, wherein a third-party compromises a trusted product to steal data, like some Ledger hardware wallets that have been sold by a reseller in Southeast Asia and Europe. Although Google did not characterize this as a supply chain attack, as it was perpetrated by the manufacturer itself and not a third-party operator, it still compromised a supposedly trusted operating system, leading to millions of victims. This incident also shows how even the simplest of devices can be used to execute complicated attacks, like how a Chinese couple hid a PC behind a fridge in a Japanese hotel and targeted 2.4 million victims.

#10503. Gemini 4 Carbon lags just behind Claude in benchmark, but wins in value

Google’s new frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, brings some welcome improvements and while it doesn’t top the charts in a new benchmark, it does provide much more bang for your buck.

SemiAnalysis, an AI research and analysis firm, recently published its new frontier-level benchmark, GDPx which includes numbers for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon model. The leaderboard includes every major frontier model from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta and details both the score and cost for each model.

The benchmark includes 206 tasks across finance, materials science, cybersecurity, software engineering, legal, biology, and several other domains (topics).

Topping the results is Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, but Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is very close behind. The difference between the two is relatively minimal, but the cost is the biggest factor to consider here. Where Claude’s cost came out to around $51 per task, Gemini was just over $16 per task. Gemini also beat the next model on the list, GPT-6 Astra, which scored lower while costing more than both at about $54 per task.

The report notes that taking out cybersecurity, biology, and alignment domains shuffles the results. Safety guardrails in Claude and GPT models puts GPT-6 Astra at the top of the list with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 outranking Gemini 4 Carbon. SemiAnalysis says that this better aligns with their “subjective impressions” of each model.

As for Google’s existing frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, it ranks in eighth place on both lists, beating Meta’s Muse Wonder, but below Wonder Full. Argon’s costs in this particular benchmark are only slightly lower than Carbon.

Both of Google’s models score better than OpenAI and Anthropic models when focused on cybersecurity, but do fall behind Meta’s Muse models, which the benchmark found to be the best “by a meaningful margin.”

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28 and touted “significant gains,” but the public release date has not been confirmed just yet. It is “coming soon” for most customers. Google’s own benchmark, below, beat GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 in many aspects.
